title: Signatures of Steerability in Activation Space of Language Models

paper.title: Signatures of Steerability in Activation Space of Language Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Steering language models using a set of contrastive representations has been a canonical and computationally efficient method for controlling model behavior. Despite this success in controlling certain model behaviors, the effectiveness of activation steering varies markedly across concepts; the generalization properties of steering vectors are often considered a function of the dataset used to construct them. We make this dataset-dependence claim more rigorous and show that simple separation metrics strongly correlate with the downstream steerability of language models across diverse settings, even after controlling for layers and dataset effects. Beyond prediction, we provide evidence from a synthetic superposition experiment that separation metrics are strongly correlated with alignment between the empirical and true feature direction. Our results suggest that simple separability statistics can serve as practical diagnostics for when steering vectors are likely to work. 1 1 1 Code available at https://github.com/x-labs-xyz/steering-signatures

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent work in language model interpretability shows that model behavior can be altered by adding a linear direction, called a steering vector , to hidden activations at inference time. Prior work has shown that such steering vectors can control honesty, harmlessness, and refusal without updating model weights, suggesting that high-level properties of model behavior are encoded, at least approximately, in a one-dimensional subspace of the representation space ( Subramani et al., 2022 ; Turner et al., 2023 ; Zou et al., 2023 ; Todd et al., 2024 ) . The initial wave of optimism about steering vectors has subsequently been dampened by recent works that have made it clear that steering is not uniformly reliable. Steering effectiveness can vary substantially across concepts, prompt templates, datasets, and intervention layers, and can degrade under reasonable distribution shift ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Da Silva et al., 2025 ) . In particular, prior analyses suggest that steerability is often better explained by properties of the source dataset than by the model, raising the possibility that a steering vector succeeds only when the target concept is cleanly expressed in the activations from which it is estimated ( Tan et al., 2024 ) . Figure 1: Signal-to-Noise ratio predicts steerability in real models (left) because it detects the recovery of the underlying behavioral direction in controlled superposition (right). Across six instruction-tuned models and 38 persona, truthfulness and safety datasets, SNR explains a substantial fraction of variance in steerability ( r = 0.76 r=0.76 ). In a synthetic setting where the ground-truth feature direction v 0 v_{0} is known by construction, SNR is strongly correlated with feature recovery π = ⟨ μ , v 0 ⟩ ‖ μ ‖ 2 ​ ( ρ = 0.91 ) \pi=\frac{\left\langle\mu,v_{0}\right\rangle}{\left\lVert\mu\right\rVert_{2}}(\rho=0.91) , but only weakly with sparsity ( ρ = − 0.33 ) (\rho=-0.33) . These observations motivate the central question of this work: Can we identify a function of the set of activations used to train steering vectors that can predict their downstream performance? In the context of steering vectors trained through Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) Rimsky et al. (2024) , we hypothesize that its downstream reliability should depend on how strongly positive and negative sets of activations are "separated" in the activation space. We make the notion of "separation" rigorous by considering metrics based on (i) directional alignment between steering vector and individual contrastive points, (ii) signal-to-noise ratios that compare the mean difference to class variances, and (iii) geometric or manifold-based measures that capture the structure of activation clouds. We show that simple separability metrics correlate consistently with steerability across model families, even after controlling for major confounders. In a synthetic superposition setup, we find that the same metrics weakly correlate with the sparsity of the superposition structure, but strongly track the directional alignment between linearly recovered and true feature vector.

sections.heading: 2.1 Predicting ability from representations
sections.text: The relationship between representational geometry and downstream capabilities has been widely studied. Prior work links phenomena such as neural collapse ( Papyan et al., 2020 ) , low intrinsic dimension ( Ansuini et al., 2019 ) , and manifold geometry ( Chou et al., 2026 ) to improved generalization and performance. These geometric diagnostics have largely been studied in image models, with limited applications in language models. Since steering operates directly in activation space, it is reasonable to expect its success to depend on properties of the underlying representations. Braun et al. (2025) show that the alignment between individual activations and the steering direction strongly correlates with steerability in Llama models. We extend this line of analysis by examining a broader set of separation metrics across multiple model families.

sections.heading: 2.2 Linear Representation Hypothesis & Superposition
sections.text: Steering is often motivated through the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH), the claim that meaningful concepts are represented as approximately linear directions in the hidden states of language models ( Park et al., 2024 ) . Empirical work overwhelmingly supports this view; compact directions in activation space have been shown to encode abstractions that are causally relevant for model outputs ( Bolukbasi et al., 2016 ; Zou et al., 2023 ; Todd et al., 2024 ) . However, LRH does not imply that every concept can be cleanly decomposed into unique orthogonal directions. A central challenge is superposition, where models represent many sparse features in overlapping subspaces ( Elhage et al., 2022 ; Arora et al., 2018 ) . Interference from superposition can become an issue for steering; even if a target concept is linearly present, the direction recovered from finite contrastive data may be contaminated by other latent factors that co-occur in the dataset. We supplement our empirical analysis with a synthetic superposition setting that enables us to explicitly investigate which aspects of superposition our separation metrics capture.

sections.heading: 3.1 Dataset & Models
sections.text: We work with 26 multiple choice persona datasets from Perez et al. (2023) , 5 truthfulness datasets from Ying et al. (2026) and 7 safety datasets from Zhang et al. (2024) . The full list of datasets is included in Appendix G . Each data point in the dataset contains a triplet 𝒟 = { x i , y i + , y i − } i = 1 n \mathcal{D}=\{x_{i},y_{i}^{+},y_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{n} where x i x_{i} is the prompt eliciting a particular persona, y + y^{+} is the desired completion and y − y^{-} is the undesired completion. For each dataset, we perform a 50-50 train-test split. The train split is used to construct the steering vector and compute activation separation metrics while steerability is computed on the test set. We experiment with instruction tuned models across two parameter scales (1B-4B and 7B-14B) and across Qwen Yang et al. (2025) , Gemma Team et al. (2025) , and Llama Grattafiori et al. (2024) model families. All experiments were conducted using PyTorch Paszke et al. (2019) and Transformers Wolf et al. (2020) on a single H100 GPU.

sections.text: For each dataset, we construct a steering vector, μ \mu , via Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ) as the mean activation difference between contrastive pairs at the last-token position of residual layer. Following Tan et al. (2024) , we measure steerability as the slope of the best linear fit between steering multiplier λ \lambda and the resulting mean propensity, m ⁡ ( x ) = logit ​ ( y + ) − logit ​ ( y − ) m(x)=\text{logit}(y^{+})-\text{logit}(y^{-}) on the test set. Intuitively, steerability captures how reliably increasing the steering strength shifts the model toward the target behavior. We provide the full mathematical details of steering vector construction and steerability in Appendix A .

Table 1 shows the model-specific correlation for all combinations of datasets and layers, while Appendix D shows the results for each family of datasets. Table 2 shows the partial correlations across models after controlling for layer and datasets. We compute partial correlations through linear residualization on the dataset or layer indicator variables, and compute the Pearson/Spearman correlation of the separation metrics with the residuals. We include details of this construction and the partial correlations in Appendix C . We consistently find that SNR is the best predictor of steerability, even after controlling for dataset and layers. SNR has the strongest Pearson and Spearman correlations across the full set of comparisons (Table 1 ) and after controlling for dataset and layer effects (Table 2 ). Mean μ \mu Alignment is competitive and generally moves alongside SNR. Manifold capacity is also broadly informative, and moves in the same direction as SNR and mean μ \mu alignment. However, it rarely surpasses SNR and mean μ \mu alignment. While broader manifold-level geometry matters, it is likely that simpler activation statistics capture the practically relevant variation more directly. Intrinsic dimension seems to be weak in all settings, indicating that the dimensionality of the manifold of the difference of activations might not be a consistent predictor of downstream steerability. Intrinsic dimension also shows an interesting dataset specific variability that is not present in the other metrics; while intrinsic dimension shows positive correlation with steerability for truthfulness (Table 9 ) and safety (Table 8 ) datasets, the sign flips and it is negative for persona datasets (Table 7 ). Its correlation also drops remarkably when controlling for layers (Table 5 ) while showing a stronger signal after controlling for datasets (Table 6 ). It is likely that the correlation of intrinsic dimension with downstream steerability is tracking a layer-dependent representational geometry, rather than a relationship that generalizes across datasets.

sections.heading: 4.2 Why separation predicts steerability?
sections.text: An open question remains: which property of the activation distribution do the separation metrics track, such that they predict downstream steerability. We use the synthetic superposition setup and the assumption of the linear representation hypothesis to ask what property of the activation distribution the separation metrics are tracking. We consider three candidate mechanisms. Under the feature-recovery hypothesis, metrics track π \pi , the cosine similarity between μ \mu and the true feature direction, and SNR predicts steerability because steering works only to the extent that μ \mu approximates the true behavioral direction. Under the sparsity hypothesis, metrics track k k , the number of active features in superposition, and sparser representations are easier to steer. Under the coherence hypothesis, metrics track ϵ \epsilon , the maximum alignment between true feature directions; more orthogonal feature dictionaries should support cleaner interventions. Table 3 shows that SNR and mean alignment strongly correlate with π \pi , have a modest negative correlation with k k and show essentially no connection with ϵ \epsilon . This lends credence to feature recovery over the other two mechanisms. The metrics that best predict steerability in real LLMs track feature recovery rather than global structural properties of superposition in the synthetic setting. Intrinsic dimension shows the opposite pattern and is the only metric showing an association with k k and ϵ \epsilon . However, the fact that intrinsic dimension is the weakest metric in real LLMs suggests that global superposition geometry is neither necessary nor sufficient for predicting steerability. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We investigate properties of the activation distributions and show that across multiple model families and datasets, simple separation statistics are strong predictors of steerability. Our synthetic superposition experiments further clarify the role of these metrics; the separation statistics only weakly capture global structural properties of superposition but they strongly track whether the recovered direction aligns with the underlying feature direction.

sections.heading: 6.1 Steering method
sections.text: We limit our analysis to CAA, one approach within a broad literature on steering vector construction. It is unclear whether the analyses presented here extend to steering methods that do not rely on the same linearity assumptions used in CAA, such as optimization-based steering or methods based on non-linear interactions.

sections.heading: 6.2 Analyses are correlative, not causal
sections.text: Our key results are based on correlations between separation metrics and downstream steerability. However, we do not extend the analysis to determine whether separation causally contributes to improved steerability. It remains unclear whether these separations reflect mechanisms the model actually exploits during steering, or if they are merely geometric properties of the representation space without direct computational relevance. It is possible that both the feature recovery mechanism we propose and steerability are caused by an unknown third variable, which drives the positive correlation we report on.

sections.heading: 6.3 Testing on specified task format
sections.text: We limit ourselves to multiple-choice datasets and evaluate steering performance based on changes in option logits. Previous work has shown that this multiple-choice propensity is generally correlated with the expression of the concept in open ended generation Rimsky et al. (2024) , however, steering has also been shown to degrade the fluency of the model on unrelated tasks Pres et al. (2024) . We do not explicitly test the change in fluency of the model in free-form generation. It remains possible that stronger separation improves steerability while degrading fluency or performance on other tasks.

sections.heading: 7 Ethical Considerations
sections.text: Our results show that geometric properties of representations can predict if steering interventions are likely to succeed. This can be used for understanding, controlling, and mitigating unwanted behaviors. However, it can also lower the barrier for adversarially manipulating language models in systematic ways. Identifying easily steerable representations can enable malicious actors to systematically induce biased and harmful behavior.

sections.heading: Appendix A Mathematical details on steerability and separation metrics
sections.text: For a dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , we construct a steering vector μ l 𝒟 \mu_{l}^{\mathcal{D}} by extracting the activations from the last token after residual layer l l . We construct two contrastive prompts; one with the positive completion a l ​ ( x , y + ) ∈ ℝ d a_{l}(x,y^{+})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and one with the negative completion a l ​ ( x , y − ) ∈ ℝ d a_{l}(x,y^{-})\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . The steering vector is constructed by taking the mean difference between the contrastive pairs. μ l 𝒟 = 1 n ​ ∑ ( x , y + , y − ) ∈ 𝒟 a l ​ ( x , y + ) − a l ​ ( x , y − ) \mu_{l}^{\mathcal{D}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{(x,y^{+},y^{-})\in\mathcal{D}}a_{l}(x,y^{+})-a_{l}(x,y^{-}) (1) To measure the success of the steering vector, we use the steerability metric as defined in Tan et al. (2024) . For a prompt x x , the propensity is defined by the logit difference of positive and negative completions, m ⁡ ( x ) = logit ​ ( y + ) − logit ​ ( y − ) m(x)=\text{logit}(y^{+})-\text{logit}(y^{-}) . Steering is applied by modifying the model activations with a scaled steering vector λ ​ μ l 𝒟 \lambda\mu_{l}^{\mathcal{D}} . We evaluate the model across a range of multipliers, λ ∈ Λ \lambda\in\Lambda and compute the average propensity m ¯ ​ ( λ , μ l 𝒟 ) \bar{m}(\lambda,\mu_{l}^{\mathcal{D}}) after steering across the test dataset. The steerability of μ l 𝒟 \mu_{l}^{\mathcal{D}} is then defined as the slope of the best linear fit between the steering strength and the resulting mean propensity: s ⁡ ( μ l 𝒟 , Λ ) = slope ​ ( λ , m ¯ ​ ( λ , μ l 𝒟 ) ) , λ ∈ Λ s(\mu_{l}^{\mathcal{D}},\Lambda)=\text{slope}\left(\lambda,\bar{m}(\lambda,\mu_{l}^{\mathcal{D}})\right),\quad\lambda\in\Lambda (2) Intuitively, Eq 2 measures how consistently increasing the steering strength moves the model toward the desired behavior. For certain personas and concepts, instruction-tuned models may exhibit an inherent propensity for the target behavior without any intervention. The steerability metric therefore captures how responsive the model is to steering beyond this baseline preference.

sections.text: For truthfulness, we use the dataset suite released by Ying et al. (2026) . The FLEED dataset ( Fictional, Logical, Empirical, Ethical, Definitional ) is a collection of balanced true/false statement pairs partitioned into five categories of factuality. Each category targets a distinct epistemic basis for the truth value of a claim. We use each of the FLEED categories as a dataset within the truthfulness family. Despite this success in controlling certain model behaviors, the effectiveness of activation steering varies markedly across concepts; the generalization properties of steering vectors are often considered a function of the dataset used to construct them. We make this dataset-dependence claim more rigorous and show that simple separation metrics strongly correlate with the downstream steerability of language models across diverse settings, even after controlling for layers and dataset effects. Beyond prediction, we provide evidence from a synthetic superposition experiment that separation metrics are strongly correlated with alignment between the empirical and true feature direction. Our results suggest that simple separability statistics can serve as practical diagnostics for when steering vectors are likely to work. 1 1 1 Code available at https://github.com/x-labs-xyz/steering-signatures 1 Introduction Recent work in language model interpretability shows that model behavior can be altered by adding a linear direction, called a steering vector , to hidden activations at inference time. Prior work has shown that such steering vectors can control honesty, harmlessness, and refusal without updating model weights, suggesting that high-level properties of model behavior are encoded, at least approximately, in a one-dimensional subspace of the representation space ( Subramani et al., 2022 ; Turner et al., 2023 ; Zou et al., 2023 ; Todd et al., 2024 ) . The initial wave of optimism about steering vectors has subsequently been dampened by recent works that have made it clear that steering is not uniformly reliable. Steering effectiveness can vary substantially across concepts, prompt templates, datasets, and intervention layers, and can degrade under reasonable distribution shift ( Tan et al., 2024 ; Da Silva et al., 2025 ) . In particular, prior analyses suggest that steerability is often better explained by properties of the source dataset than by the model, raising the possibility that a steering vector succeeds only when the target concept is cleanly expressed in the activations from which it is estimated ( Tan et al., 2024 ) . Figure 1: Signal-to-Noise ratio predicts steerability in real models (left) because it detects the recovery of the underlying behavioral direction in controlled superposition (right). Across six instruction-tuned models and 38 persona, truthfulness and safety datasets, SNR explains a substantial fraction of variance in steerability ( r = 0.76 r=0.76 ). In a synthetic setting where the ground-truth feature direction v 0 v_{0} is known by construction, SNR is strongly correlated with feature recovery π = ⟨ μ , v 0 ⟩ ‖ μ ‖ 2 ​ ( ρ = 0.91 ) \pi= rac{\left\langle\mu,v_{0}ightangle}{\left\lVert\muightVert_{2}}(ho=0.91) , but only weakly with sparsity ( ρ = − 0.33 ) (ho=-0.33) . These observations motivate the central question of this work: Can we identify a function of the set of activations used to train steering vectors that can predict their downstream performance? In the context of steering vectors trained through Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) Rimsky et al. (2024) , we hypothesize that its downstream reliability should depend on how strongly positive and negative sets of activations are "separated" in the activation space. We make the notion of "separation" rigorous by considering metrics based on (i) directional alignment between steering vector and individual contrastive points, (ii) signal-to-noise ratios that compare the mean difference to class variances, and (iii) geometric or manifold-based measures that capture the structure of activation clouds. We show that simple separability metrics correlate consistently with steerability across model families, even after controlling for major confounders. In a synthetic superposition setup, we find that the same metrics weakly correlate with the sparsity of the superposition structure, but strongly track the directional alignment between linearly recovered and true feature vector. 2 Background 2.1 Predicting ability from representations The relationship between representational geometry and downstream capabilities has been widely studied. Prior work links phenomena such as neural collapse ( Papyan et al., 2020 ) , low intrinsic dimension ( Ansuini et al., 2019 ) , and manifold geometry ( Chou et al., 2026 ) to improved generalization and performance. These geometric diagnostics have largely been studied in image models, with limited applications in language models. Since steering operates directly in activation space, it is reasonable to expect its success to depend on properties of the underlying representations. Braun et al. (2025) show that the alignment between individual activations and the steering direction strongly correlates with steerability in Llama models. We extend this line of analysis by examining a broader set of separation metrics across multiple model families. 2.2 Linear Representation Hypothesis & Superposition Steering is often motivated through the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH), the claim that meaningful concepts are represented as approximately linear directions in the hidden states of language models ( Park et al., 2024 ) . Empirical work overwhelmingly supports this view; compact directions in activation space have been shown to encode abstractions that are causally relevant for model outputs ( Bolukbasi et al., 2016 ; Zou et al., 2023 ; Todd et al., 2024 ) . However, LRH does not imply that every concept can be cleanly decomposed into unique orthogonal directions. A central challenge is superposition, where models represent many sparse features in overlapping subspaces ( Elhage et al., 2022 ; Arora et al., 2018 ) . Interference from superposition can become an issue for steering; even if a target concept is linearly present, the direction recovered from finite contrastive data may be contaminated by other latent factors that co-occur in the dataset. We supplement our empirical analysis with a synthetic superposition setting that enables us to explicitly investigate which aspects of superposition our separation metrics capture. 3 Methods 3.1 Dataset & Models We work with 26 multiple choice persona datasets from Perez et al. (2023) , 5 truthfulness datasets from Ying et al. (2026) and 7 safety datasets from Zhang et al. (2024) . The full list of datasets is included in Appendix G . The train split is used to construct the steering vector and compute activation separation metrics while steerability is computed on the test set. We consistently find that SNR is the best predictor of steerability, even after controlling for dataset and layers. SNR has the strongest Pearson and Spearman correlations across the full set of comparisons (Table 1 ) and after controlling for dataset and layer effects (Table 2 ). Mean μ \mu Alignment is competitive and generally moves alongside SNR. Manifold capacity is also broadly informative, and moves in the same direction as SNR and mean μ \mu alignment. However, it rarely surpasses SNR and mean μ \mu alignment. While broader manifold-level geometry matters, it is likely that simpler activation statistics capture the practically relevant variation more directly. Intrinsic dimension seems to be weak in all settings, indicating that the dimensionality of the manifold of the difference of activations might not be a consistent predictor of downstream steerability. Intrinsic dimension also shows an interesting dataset specific variability that is not present in the other metrics; while intrinsic dimension shows positive correlation with steerability for truthfulness (Table 9 ) and safety (Table 8 ) datasets, the sign flips and it is negative for persona datasets (Table 7 ). An open question remains: which property of the activation distribution do the separation metrics track, such that they predict downstream steerability. We use the synthetic superposition setup and the assumption of the linear representation hypothesis to ask what property of the activation distribution the separation metrics are tracking. We consider three candidate mechanisms. Under the feature-recovery hypothesis, metrics track π \pi , the cosine similarity between μ \mu and the true feature direction, and SNR predicts steerability because steering works only to the extent that μ \mu approximates the true behavioral direction. Under the sparsity hypothesis, metrics track k k , the number of active features in superposition, and sparser representations are easier to steer. Under the coherence hypothesis, metrics track ϵ \epsilon , the maximum alignment between true feature directions; more orthogonal feature dictionaries should support cleaner interventions. Table 3 shows that SNR and mean alignment strongly correlate with π \pi , have a modest negative correlation with k k and show essentially no connection with ϵ \epsilon . This lends credence to feature recovery over the other two mechanisms. The metrics that best predict steerability in real LLMs track feature recovery rather than global structural properties of superposition in the synthetic setting. Intrinsic dimension shows the opposite pattern and is the only metric showing an association with k k and ϵ \epsilon . However, the fact that intrinsic dimension is the weakest metric in real LLMs suggests that global superposition geometry is neither necessary nor sufficient for predicting steerability. Our synthetic superposition experiments further clarify the role of these metrics; the separation statistics only weakly capture global structural properties of superposition but they strongly track whether the recovered direction aligns with the underlying feature direction. 6 Limitations 6.1 Steering method We limit our analysis to CAA, one approach within a broad literature on steering vector construction. It is unclear whether the analyses presented here extend to steering methods that do not rely on the same linearity assumptions used in CAA, such as optimization-based steering or methods based on non-linear interactions. 6.2 Analyses are correlative, not causal Our key results are based on correlations between separation metrics and downstream steerability. However, we do not extend the analysis to determine whether separation causally contributes to improved steerability. It remains unclear whether these separations reflect mechanisms the model actually exploits during steering, or if they are merely geometric properties of the representation space without direct computational relevance. It is possible that both the feature recovery mechanism we propose and steerability are caused by an unknown third variable, which drives the positive correlation we report on. 6.3 Testing on specified task format We limit ourselves to multiple-choice datasets and evaluate steering performance based on changes in option logits. Previous work has shown that this multiple-choice propensity is generally correlated with the expression of the concept in open ended generation Rimsky et al. (2024) , however, steering has also been shown to degrade the fluency of the model on unrelated tasks Pres et al. (2024) . We do not explicitly test the change in fluency of the model in free-form generation. It remains possible that stronger separation improves steerability while degrading fluency or performance on other tasks. 7 Ethical Considerations Our results show that geometric properties of representations can predict if steering interventions are likely to succeed. This can be used for understanding, controlling, and mitigating unwanted behaviors. However, it can also lower the barrier for adversarially manipulating language models in systematic ways. Identifying easily steerable representations can enable malicious actors to systematically induce biased and harmful behavior. 8 AI use statement We utilized AI assistants for literature search, polishing the language of the paper and coding. The FLEED dataset ( Fictional, Logical, Empirical, Ethical, Definitional ) is a collection of balanced true/false statement pairs partitioned into five categories of factuality. Each category targets a distinct epistemic basis for the truth value of a claim. We use each of the FLEED categories as a dataset within the truthfulness family. Table 14 include the details of each category. Category Kind of factuality Definitional Claims whose truth follows from the meaning of the constituent terms (e.g. “A triangle has three sides”). Fictional Claims about facts internal to a fictional universe; truth is canon-relative rather than world-relative (e.g. “Frodo carried the One Ring to Mordor”).
